reason: E3 directly states that multiple principal elements in HEAs can segregate to grain boundaries and that Cr-rich phases can form there, supporting the first two premises. However, the cited evidence does not show that this segregation occurs as nanoclusters that reduce cohesion without forming identifiable intermetallic phases, nor does it demonstrate that pre-existing precipitates act as sinks to retain ductility. E1 and E2 discuss impurity-driven effects and conventional intermetallic precipitation, which do not support the proposed distinct mechanism.
premises: Principal elements (Cr, Mn, Ni) can segregate to grain boundaries in HEAs
This segregation can form nanoclusters rather than conventional precipitates
Such nanoclustering reduces grain-boundary cohesion and causes brittle intergranular fracture
This mechanism is distinct from impurity- or precipitate-induced embrittlement in conventional alloys
Pre-existing Cr-rich precipitates can act as sinks to suppress detrimental segregation
